newsitem.title: USA: Stock funds seen returning 10-12 percent in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Stock funds seen returning 10-12 percent in 1997.

text.p: U.S. mutual funds will experience more modest returns in 1997 compared with the robust stretch in 1995-1996, fund tracker Michael Lipper predicted Wednesday.
Lipper, president of Lipper Analytical Services, forecast returns of 10 percent to 12 percent for general stock funds.
"I'm looking for a return to historical comparisons," around that level, Lipper told reporters at a press briefing.
Through Dec. 12, the general stock fund has returned an average 18.03 percent year to date vs. an average stock fund return last year of 31.08 percent.
For the five-year period from 1991 to 1996, stock funds have returned a cumulative 105.99 percent.
Lipper said that he expected fixed-income funds to post modest gains in 1997, likely no more than the value of their "coupons," or yield of the bonds that the fund holds.

In answer to a question, Lipper said he expected assets in money market funds to grow next year. Lipper said some of that growth may come from investors who sell holdings in stock funds, especially growth funds.

According to the Investment Company Institute, an industry trade group, money market funds had assets of $876 billion at the end of October. Stock mutual funds assets totalled $1.65 trillion, and bond funds had assets of $866 billion.
While there will continue to be a healthy flow of cash into funds next year, Lipper said he expected the stream to slow next year from this year's pace.
He said that the majority of Fortune 500 companies have completed conversions from defined benefit to defined contribution retirement plans, which have been a major source of cash into funds.
The companies provided most of the workers' pension contributions in defined benefit plans but under defined contribution systems, the employees must add some money.
The conversions provided a one-time giant push of money into funds.

Lipper predicted that if the U.S. stock market were flat to slightly higher, world stock funds would outperform U.S. equity funds. World equity funds have returned about 10.45 percent so far this year.
He said that if the market declined, he would expect technology sector funds to be especially hard hit, and take about 28 months to recover.
